column2:
Your platform team maintains four internal agents: support triage, a sales assistant, an engineering copilot, and an ops bot. Each one hand-authors its own tool schemas and wrapper functions for the same ticket-tracker API, roughly 30 duplicated tool definitions per agent. A recent change to the tracker API forced coordinated fixes across all four codebases.

What is the primary architectural benefit of replacing these per-agent integrations with a single ticket-tracker MCP server?

A. Each agent's model selects the tracker's tools more accurately from the server's schemas than from the hand-written ones used today.
B. The MCP server converses with the model directly in place of each agent's own agentic loop, and the agents stop managing tool calls.
C. The tracker's tool schemas and implementations are written and maintained once in the server, and each agent uses them through an MCP client.
D. MCP replaces tool use, and each model calls the tracker's API directly instead of emitting tool-use requests for the agent code to execute.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. MCP's core value is shifting the burden of defining and executing tools from each application to a dedicated server: the tracker integration is written and maintained in one place, and every agent discovers and calls the same pre-built tools through its client. Option A misstates what MCP changes; the schemas are ordinary tool schemas, and MCP does not by itself alter selection accuracy. Option B is wrong because each agent still runs its own conversation loop with the model; MCP only changes where tools live and run. Option D confuses the relationship: MCP is complementary to tool use, and the model still emits tool-use requests that are executed via the MCP client and server.

column2:
You configure Claude Desktop to connect to three MCP servers: an internal docs server, a ticket tracker, and a read-only database. A teammate reviewing your architecture diagram asks why it shows three MCP clients when there is only one application.

Which statement correctly describes the relationship?

A. Claude Desktop keeps one shared MCP client that multiplexes the three servers over a single connection opened at startup.
B. Claude Desktop is the host, and it creates one MCP client per server, each maintaining a dedicated connection to its own server.
C. Claude Desktop runs one MCP client per category of tool, and each client executes the tools in its category on the local machine.
D. Claude Desktop runs one active client for the three servers and keeps two spare clients as failover standbys in case that connection drops.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. In MCP's architecture the host is the AI application, and it creates one client for each server it connects to, with each client holding a dedicated one-to-one connection — three servers therefore means three clients. Option A describes a multiplexing model MCP does not use. Option C is doubly wrong: clients do not execute tools (servers do), and clients map to servers, not tool categories. Option D invents a redundancy scheme; multiple clients are the normal connection model, not standbys.

References:
• MCP architecture — Participants
• MCP spec: architecture — Clients

column2:
You are building an MCP server that exposes an engineer's on-laptop development database to Claude Code. The server will run on the same machine, launched by Claude Code as a subprocess at the start of each session.

Which transport is the standard fit for this deployment?

A. The stdio transport, with Claude Code writing messages to the server's standard input and reading replies from its standard output.
B. The Streamable HTTP transport, with Claude Code sending each message as an HTTP POST to a network endpoint that the server exposes.
C. The WebSocket transport, with Claude Code holding a persistent bidirectional connection to a URL on which the server listens.
D. The SSE transport, with Claude Code connecting to a URL where the server streams its messages over a long-lived HTTP connection.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. stdio is the transport designed for exactly this shape: a local server that the host launches as a subprocess, with the two exchanging messages over standard input and output on the same machine and no network in the path. Option B names Streamable HTTP, the transport for remote servers that typically serve many clients; Claude Code connects to such a server at its URL and treats it as remote instead of launching it. Option C names the WebSocket server type that Claude Code offers for remote servers that push events to Claude unprompted; it is configured with a URL, and the MCP specification's standard transports are stdio and Streamable HTTP. Option D names SSE, which Claude Code documents as deprecated in favor of HTTP and which, like Options B and C, connects to a remote endpoint rather than starting a local process.

column2:
Your team wrote its docs MCP server with the Python SDK. A sister team's agent is written in TypeScript, and it connects to your server and uses every tool without any changes on your side. An engineer asks how this works across languages.

What makes this interoperability possible?

A. The standard transports, stdio and Streamable HTTP, define the format of the tool-call messages that both SDKs send and receive.
B. Claude detects the language each server is written in and adapts the format of its tool calls to match before emitting them.
C. The client reads the server's source code when it connects and generates typed bindings for its own language from that source.
D. The MCP spec defines JSON-RPC messages, such as list-tools and call-tool, that clients and servers implement in their own languages.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. MCP's data layer is a JSON-RPC based exchange whose message types are defined by the specification; both sides speak that wire protocol, so implementation language is irrelevant. Option A confuses the layers: stdio and Streamable HTTP are transports that carry messages between the two sides, while the data layer is what defines those messages, so the choice of transport does not explain cross-language compatibility. Option B places the adaptation in the model, but the model never talks to servers directly and the message format does not vary by language. Option C describes code generation that does not happen; the client learns about a server through protocol messages like the list-tools request, not by reading its source.

column2:
The team that owns your company's ticket-tracker MCP server ships four new tools overnight. The next morning your support agent, whose own code has not been redeployed, starts using all four tools in conversations.

Why are the new tools available without an agent release?

A. The agent's .mcp.json file caches every connected server's tool schemas and was regenerated automatically when the server changed.
B. The agent sends a list-tools request when it connects, so each session offers the model whatever the server currently exposes.
C. Anthropic refreshed the model's weights overnight, so the model itself now knows about the four new tool definitions.
D. The agent's build pipeline embeds server schemas at compile time, and a scheduled nightly rebuild picked up the new tool definitions.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. Tool definitions are not baked into the client; the client asks the server what it offers each time it connects, so server-side additions appear in the very next session. Option A misunderstands the config file, which stores how to connect to servers, not their tool schemas. Option C attributes the change to the model, but models learn about available tools from the definitions sent with each request, not from retraining. Option D contradicts the stem — no redeploy occurred — and describes exactly the build-time embedding that MCP's runtime discovery replaces.

• MCP architecture — Primitives
• Build an MCP client — How it works

column2:
In a design review for a GitHub-connected assistant, a colleague objects: 'We can already give Claude tools that call the GitHub API directly — MCP just adds moving parts.' Covering repositories, pull requests, and issues would take your team roughly 25 hand-built tools.

What is the most accurate response?

A. MCP is required for this integration, and tools that your own team writes have no way to call an external API on their own.
B. MCP improves tool-selection accuracy, and models choose more reliably among server-defined tools than among hand-written ones.
C. Direct tool use is deprecated in favor of MCP, and new integrations are expected to define their tools in servers instead.
D. MCP complements tool use, and those 25 tools are authored and maintained in a server that your team connects to rather than builds.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. The honest case for MCP is about ownership and maintenance, not new model capability: the same tools exist either way, but with MCP they are written, executed, and updated inside a server your team merely connects to, such as the official integrations that companies maintain for their own platforms. Option A is false — hand-authored tools calling GitHub directly work fine, which is exactly the colleague's point. Option B claims an accuracy benefit MCP does not promise; selection quality depends on the definitions, not on who hosts them. Option C is wrong because tool use is not deprecated; MCP builds on it, and the model still makes ordinary tool calls.

column2:
Your ticket-tracker MCP server must support two consumers: individual engineers running Claude Code on their laptops, and a centrally hosted support agent that serves about 40 concurrent users from one deployment.

Which TWO transport and deployment decisions are correct? (Select TWO.)

A. Avoid HTTP for both consumers, because the MCP specification defines stdio as the only standard transport a server may use.
B. Point each laptop's stdio transport at the central host over the network, since stdio connections work across machines as well.
C. Run a Streamable HTTP server for the central deployment, since that transport is designed for remote servers serving many clients.
D. For the laptops, ship a local server that each Claude Code instance launches itself and communicates with over stdio.
column3:
Correct Answer: C and D. Options C and D pair each deployment with its intended transport: stdio is for local, same-machine processes where the host spawns the server, while Streamable HTTP is for remote servers that typically serve many clients at once. Option B is impossible as stated — stdio is standard input/output between processes on one machine, not a network protocol. Option A is factually wrong; the spec defines both stdio and Streamable HTTP transports, and a remote multi-user deployment is exactly where the HTTP transport belongs.

column2:
Your internal docs MCP server uses the Python SDK and defines 14 tools. The team also hand-maintains a separate JSON schema file per tool, and two production incidents last month traced to a schema advertising a parameter its function no longer accepts.

What is the most effective way to eliminate this class of drift?

A. Add a nightly CI job that diffs each tool's advertised inputSchema against its function's signature and fails the build on a mismatch.
B. Define each tool as an @mcp.tool-decorated function with typed parameters and Field descriptions that the SDK turns into the schema.
C. Drop the schema files and describe each tool's parameters in prose in its description field, leaving the model to read the input format there.
D. Keep both artifacts and set additionalProperties to false in each hand-written schema to reject any parameter that the schema does not declare.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. The Python SDK generates the JSON schema directly from the decorated function's type hints and Field descriptions, so the signature is the single source of truth and schema-versus-code drift cannot occur. Option A builds tooling to police a duplication the SDK makes unnecessary; it detects drift but still leaves two artifacts to keep in sync. Option C moves the parameter contract out of inputSchema and into free text in description, removing machine-enforced structure and trading a solved problem for probabilistic parsing of prose. Option D tightens validation for parameters the schema does not declare, but the incidents involved a parameter the schema still declared after its function dropped it, so the stale advertisement would remain.

column2:
Your docs server exposes search_docs, which takes keywords and returns matching document IDs, and read_doc_contents, which returns one document by exact ID. Each has a one-line description: 'Searches documents' and 'Reads a document.' In test transcripts, the agent calls read_doc_contents with guessed, nonexistent IDs in about 20% of tasks instead of searching first.

What is the most effective first change?

A. Add a routing layer that classifies each user request and restricts which of the two tools the model is allowed to call for it.
B. Merge both into one find_or_read tool that falls back to keyword search whenever the given ID fails to resolve to a document.
C. Rewrite both descriptions to say what input each expects, keywords or an exact ID returned by a prior search, and when to use each.
D. Add eight few-shot example transcripts to the system prompt that demonstrate the correct search-then-read sequence for typical tasks.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. Tool descriptions are the primary signal the model uses for tool selection, and these say nothing about where a valid ID comes from; stating that read_doc_contents requires an exact ID produced by search_docs fixes the root cause at the cheapest point. Option A is over-engineered before the zero-cost fix is tried and bypasses the model's own selection ability. Option B is a redesign rather than a first change: merging tools can be a valid design, but it takes server work and hides the guessed IDs behind a fallback instead of telling the model where a valid ID comes from. Option D adds standing token overhead to compensate for definitions that remain ambiguous, treating the symptom rather than the source.

column2:
Your support application does two things with customer data: it loads the customer's account summary into the first prompt of every single session, and it occasionally needs to search past tickets when the conversation calls for it.

How should these two needs map onto your MCP server design?

A. Expose ticket search as a tool the model invokes when it judges necessary, and the account summary as a resource the application reads at session start.
B. Expose both as tools and add a system-prompt rule that the model must always call the account-summary tool before doing anything else in the session.
C. Expose both as resources, since account summaries and ticket search results are read-only customer data that application code can fetch on demand.
D. Expose ticket search as a tool and the account summary as a second tool, letting the model decide each session whether the summary is worth loading.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. The dividing line is who decides when the operation runs: ticket search depends on conversational judgment, so it belongs to the model as a tool, while the summary load happens every session unconditionally, so application code should perform it deterministically rather than hoping the model does. Option B enforces a deterministic requirement through prompt instructions, which is probabilistic where a guarantee is available. Option C breaks the search case — only the model knows mid-conversation when searching is warranted, and app code cannot anticipate it. Option D delegates a step that must happen 100% of the time to a probabilistic chooser.

column2:
A ticket-tracker MCP server exposes get_data, its replacement get_data_v2, and fetch_info. The first two search tickets by keyword, and the third returns one ticket's full details. Logs show the model splitting equivalent requests across all three, and 15% of calls still go to the deprecated get_data.

What is the most effective fix?

A. Keep the names and add a system-prompt note explaining what each of the three variants actually does and when the model should prefer it.
B. Add a keyword-based pre-parser that maps each user's phrasing to the correct tool before the model ever sees the request or the tool list.
C. Delete get_data_v2 and fetch_info so that only one tool remains for the model to call, regardless of what each of the three does.
D. Rename the tools to distinct, purpose-revealing names such as search_tickets and get_ticket_details, each described by when it applies.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. Names and descriptions are the interface the model selects against; three near-synonymous labels give it nothing to discriminate on, so renaming to distinct, intent-revealing names with matching descriptions removes the ambiguity at its source. Option A leaves the confusing surface intact and patches it with standing prompt text, a weaker and costlier signal. Option B is an over-engineered bypass of the model's language understanding for a problem caused by bad labels. Option C consolidates blindly — if the tools do different jobs, collapsing them discards capability instead of clarifying it.

• Define tools (schemas, descriptions) — Best practices for tool definitions

column2:
You are defining process_refund for a customer-support resolution agent. Refund mistakes are costly, and the tool will sit alongside get_customer and lookup_order on the same MCP server.

Which TWO elements of the tool definition contribute most to reliable use by the model? (Select TWO.)

A. A title field that gives the tool a human-readable name for display purposes in client interfaces.
B. Typed, constrained parameters — order ID, amount, reason — declared in the input schema with a description for each.
C. A description stating what the tool does, its prerequisites such as a verified customer, and how it differs from the lookup tools.
D. An annotations object with destructiveHint set to true, describing the refund as a destructive action.
column3:
Correct Answer: B and C. Option B makes the expected input machine-checkable and tells the model exactly what to supply, and Option C is the steering surface that governs when the model reaches for this tool rather than its neighbors — together they cover the two failure modes that matter most for a high-stakes action: malformed calls and misselection. Option A adds a name meant for people: the spec defines title as a human-readable name for display purposes, and it tells the model nothing about when to call the tool or what to pass. Option D adds a hint about the tool's behavior that is addressed to clients, which the spec has them treat as untrusted unless the server is trusted; neither the inputs to supply nor the conditions for choosing the tool are stated there, which is the job of the schema and the description.

column2:
A teammate proposes collapsing your document server's read_doc_contents and edit_document tools into one document_op tool with an action parameter set to 'read' or 'edit', plus optional old_string and new_string fields, arguing that fewer tools are always easier for the model.

What is the strongest reason to keep the two separate tools?

A. The MCP specification caps the size of a tool's input schema, and a combined tool carrying both read and edit parameters would exceed that limit.
B. Each operation keeps its own precise schema and description, so a read cannot carry edit-only parameters and each tool has one clear contract.
C. A combined tool could not validate its inputs or raise an execution error for a missing document, since validation only works on single-purpose schemas.
D. Keeping two tools halves the token cost of tool definitions in every request, because two small schemas take less space than one combined schema.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. One tool per distinct operation keeps each contract precise. The edit schema can require old_string and new_string, the read schema cannot accept them, and each description covers exactly one behavior, whereas a mode flag needs optional fields that are valid only some of the time. Option A invents a limit; the specification sets no cap on input schema size, and a merged schema would be modest anyway. Option C is false; a merged tool could still validate its inputs and return execution errors, just with murkier conditional rules. Option D has the arithmetic backwards: two definitions each carry their own name, description and document parameter, so they are no cheaper than one merged definition, and the benefit is clarity, not size. Currency note (Oct 2026): Anthropic's current tool-definition guidance also recommends consolidating closely related actions into a single tool with an action parameter to reduce selection ambiguity, so treat the split as a trade-off rather than a rule, while the exam guide favors purpose-specific tools with defined input and output contracts.

column2:
Your edit_document tool performs exact find-and-replace with doc_id, old_string, and new_string parameters. In production, roughly 30% of edits silently change nothing because the model supplies old_string values with paraphrased wording or normalized whitespace that never match the document.

What is the most effective first fix?

A. Give old_string a Field description stating that the text must match the document exactly, including whitespace, copied verbatim from a prior read.
B. Wrap the edit in a server-side loop that retries up to five times with the same arguments whenever the replacement leaves the document unchanged.
C. Upgrade to a larger model, since the paraphrasing comes from limited model capability and stronger models reproduce source text verbatim unprompted.
D. Make the server fuzzy-match old_string and silently apply the replacement at the closest location it finds, so that an edit can never be a no-op.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. Parameter-level descriptions steer how the model constructs arguments; the model paraphrases because nothing tells it exact matching is required, so documenting the exact-match contract — including whitespace — on the parameter fixes the failure where it originates. Option B re-submits the same doomed arguments; retrying without new information cannot change the outcome. Option C reaches for a bigger model to compensate for an unstated requirement no model can reliably infer. Option D trades silent no-ops for something worse: silent approximate edits that can alter text the user never intended.

column2:
Your MCP server's lookup_order tool receives a well-formed call from the model, but the order number argument is in the wrong format: the tool expects eight digits and the model sent ORD-4417. You are deciding how the server should report the failure so the agent can recover.

Which reporting mechanism is correct for this case?

A. A JSON-RPC response that carries an error object naming the malformed order number in its message.
B. A normal result with isError: false and an empty content array, returned in place of an order record.
C. A result flagged isError: true whose content text states the expected eight-digit order-number format.
D. An HTTP 400 Bad Request response from the server's endpoint, with the validation message in the response body.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. The spec distinguishes protocol errors — structural problems like unknown tools or malformed requests — from tool execution errors such as input validation failures, which are returned inside the result with isError: true and actionable text precisely so the model can self-correct. A wrong order-number value inside a well-formed call is an execution error, and Option C handles it that way. Option A misclassifies it: the JSON-RPC request itself is valid, and protocol errors are the category models are least able to fix. Option B silently fabricates an empty success, hiding the failure the model needs to see. Option D answers at the HTTP layer, but the spec has a request's outcome come back as a JSON-RPC response, and a tool's own validation failure belongs inside that result where the model can see it.

References:
• MCP spec: tools — Error handling
• MCP Python SDK: handling errors — Which one to raise

column2:
Telemetry on your support agent shows process_refund failing in 18% of attempts. Every failure returns the same text: 'Error: operation failed.' In transcripts the model responds by retrying the identical call, then apologizing to the customer without resolving anything.

What change most improves the agent's recovery rate?

A. Return a neutral 'request received' acknowledgment in place of the error and let the model move on without retrying the refund call.
B. Cap tool retries at one in the client and route each failed refund directly to a human review queue with the transcript attached.
C. Ask the model to rate its own confidence after each failure, retry when the rating exceeds 0.8, and escalate to a human otherwise.
D. Return error text naming the failed check, the offending value and a next step, such as 'over the $500 unverified limit (verify first)'.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Tool execution errors are supposed to carry actionable feedback the model can use to adjust and retry; a generic status gives it nothing, which is why it repeats the same call. Option D supplies the missing information — which rule failed, on what value, and what to do next — enabling genuine self-correction. Option A is silent suppression: the model will tell the customer the refund succeeded. Option B escalates every failure, including the large fraction the model could fix itself once informed, and still leaves the error text useless. Option C leans on self-reported confidence, which is not a reliable routing signal and adds no new facts about the failure.

References:
• MCP spec: tools — Error handling
• Handle tool calls — Handling errors with is_error
• Writing tools for agents (Anthropic engineering) — Optimizing tool responses for token efficiency

column2:
Your ticket-tracker tool has two failure modes: upstream timeouts, about 60% of errors and usually resolving within seconds, and invalid ticket IDs, the remaining 40%. Both currently return 'Error: request failed.' The agent retries invalid IDs pointlessly and abandons timed-out requests that a retry would have completed.

How should the server's error results change?

A. Distinguish the cases in the error result, marking timeouts as transient and retryable and invalid IDs as validation errors needing a corrected ID.
B. Report the timeouts as successful results with no ticket data, and keep the invalid-ID responses flagged as errors for the model to see.
C. Mark both kinds of error as retryable and have the client retry failed calls three times with exponential backoff before surfacing the failure.
D. Return an empty ticket object for both failure modes and leave the model to decide on its own whether to retry that ticket lookup later.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. The two failure classes demand opposite recoveries — retry the transient one, change strategy on the validation one — so the error result must say which class occurred and what to do about it; that is what makes an error actionable. Option B mislabels a failure as success, leaving the model to treat missing data as a completed lookup. Option C burns retries on invalid IDs that can never succeed and still gives the model no guidance afterward. Option D silently suppresses both errors and hands the model fabricated empty data, the least recoverable outcome of all.

References:
• MCP spec: tools — Error handling
• Handle tool calls — Handling errors with is_error
• Writing tools for agents (Anthropic engineering) — Optimizing tool responses for token efficiency

column2:
You built a custom MCP client for an internal agent. When a tool result arrives flagged isError: true, the client swallows it and sends Claude the text 'tool temporarily unavailable' no matter what the actual message said. Evals show the agent re-attempting the same malformed call for three consecutive turns.

What should the client do instead?

A. Convert each errored tool result into a JSON-RPC protocol error and handle the failure at the transport layer instead of in the conversation.
B. Pass the execution error's actual content through to the model as the tool result, leaving it to adjust its arguments or change approach.
C. Drop the errored tool calls and their results from the conversation history and let the model try a different approach with a clean context.
D. Terminate the session after the first errored call and restart the conversation from scratch with a fresh context and an empty history.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. Clients should surface tool execution errors to the model because that feedback is what enables self-correction; this client replaces a presumably specific message with a misleading generic one, so the model keeps repeating a call it believes merely hit a temporary outage. Option A moves the failure into the protocol-error category, the kind models are least equipped to act on, and hides it from the conversation. Option C removes even the evidence that something failed, guaranteeing repetition. Option D throws away the whole session over a routine recoverable failure rather than letting the model retry with better arguments.

References:
• MCP spec: tools — Error handling
• Handle tool calls — Handling errors with is_error

column2:
Your docs MCP server must support a client UI that lists all document IDs in an autocomplete menu and fetches one document's contents when the user mentions it. There are about 200 documents averaging 4 KB each.

How should the server expose this data?

A. One direct resource, docs://documents, that returns the full text of all 200 documents in a single read for the client to search itself.
B. One templated resource, docs://documents/{doc_id}, that the client reads once for each possible ID to build its autocomplete menu.
C. Two tools, list_docs and read_doc, that the application has the model call on its behalf whenever the UI needs fresh data for the menu.
D. Two resources, a direct docs://documents that returns the document IDs and a templated docs://documents/{doc_id} that returns one document.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. The working pattern is one resource per distinct read operation: a static listing gets a direct (fixed-URI) resource, and fetch-one-by-ID gets a templated resource whose URI parameter selects the document. Option A ships roughly 800 KB of content to draw a menu that needs only names. Option B has no listing operation at all — the client cannot know which IDs exist to iterate, and hundreds of reads to build a menu is wasteful. Option C routes app-controlled UI data through model tool calls, adding latency and a probabilistic dependency to something application code should fetch deterministically.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.4

References:
• MCP server concepts — How resources work
• MCP spec: resources — Resource templates
• MCP Python SDK: resources — Resource templates

column2:
In the Python SDK you define a templated resource with @mcp.resource('docs://documents/{doc_id}'), but the decorated function's signature is def fetch_doc(document_id: str). The server raises an error at startup while registering this resource.

What is wrong?

A. The function parameter has to be named doc_id, matching the {doc_id} placeholder that the SDK fills in from the URI.
B. The function has to take the whole requested uri as its only argument and extract the document ID from it by itself.
C. A resource that takes a parameter has to be registered with @mcp.tool instead of @mcp.resource, with the ID as an argument.
D. The ID parameter has to be annotated int, with the function converting it to text inside its body once the SDK passes it in.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. With templated resources the SDK does the URI parsing for you: each name inside braces must correspond to a function parameter of exactly that name, because the value parsed from the requested URI is passed as that keyword argument. The SDK checks this correspondence when the decorator registers the template and raises on a mismatch, so {doc_id} needs a doc_id parameter, not document_id. Option B describes the manual parsing the SDK exists to eliminate. Option C confuses the primitives: a resource template is the resource primitive's own way of taking a parameter, so a function that needs one is not moved to a tool. Option D invents a type restriction; string parameters are the normal case.

Your CLI chat app connects to a docs MCP server. Typing the @ character must instantly display the server's current list of documents in an autocomplete menu, before any message is sent to Claude.

Which MCP primitive should back this feature, and why?

A. A tool that the model calls on its own initiative whenever it judges that the interface is likely to need the document list.
B. A prompt that returns the document list to the client inside a pre-written assistant message that the client renders as the menu.
C. A resource that application code reads whenever it needs the document list, rendering the menu itself without involving the model.
D. A system-prompt preamble that lists every document and is refreshed whenever the server process restarts, before the model reads it.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. Autocomplete at keystroke time is a pure application concern — the app knows the moment it needs the data and simply reads it — which is exactly the app-controlled role resources fill; populating a document picker is a canonical use of resources. Option A cannot work: no model is running when the user types @, and tools put timing under the model's control. Option B misuses prompts, which are user-invoked message templates for workflows, not a data feed. Option D goes stale between restarts and pays for the full listing in every request whether or not the menu is opened.

column2:
Transcript analysis of your docs chatbot shows that in 70% of conversations the user names the exact document they want, as in 'summarize @report.pdf.' The agent still makes two tool round trips per request — one to list documents, one to read the named one — adding about four seconds of latency.

Which change best removes this overhead for those conversations?

A. Instruct the model in the system prompt to skip the listing call and read the named document directly whenever the user has already named one.
B. When the user mentions a document, have the application read it as an MCP resource and place the contents directly in the prompt sent to Claude.
C. Move to a model with a larger context window, so that each tool round trip carries less overhead and completes faster.
D. Cache the full contents of every document in the system prompt when the session starts, so the model never needs to list or read anything.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. When the user has already identified the document, fetching it is deterministic — application code can read the resource and inject the contents into the prompt, eliminating both exploratory tool calls; this is the same mention pattern Claude Code uses for MCP resources. Option A is prompt-level guidance that still leaves at least one model-driven round trip and no guarantee. Option C confuses context capacity with round-trip latency; window size does not make tool cycles faster. Option D front-loads every document into every request, exploding token cost and going stale as documents change.

column2:
Your direct resource docs://documents returns a Python list of IDs; the SDK serializes the return value, and the server declares MIME type application/json. In your client, the autocomplete menu renders a single entry containing the literal text ["report.pdf", "plan.md", ...] instead of one entry per document.

What is the root cause?

A. The client ignores the declared mimeType and should deserialize the returned text with json.loads before rendering.
B. The server should put the list directly in the contents array instead of serializing it into a text string first.
C. The IDs need a templated resource, with the client calling resources/read once for each document ID to build the menu.
D. The client should pass the returned text string to the model and ask it to produce one menu entry per document.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. This resource's contents arrive as text, and the MIME type is the server's hint about how to interpret that text; a client that sees application/json must parse the JSON string into a data structure, which this client is skipping. Option B fights the protocol: resource contents carry either text or binary data, so a list has to be serialized into a string before it goes on the wire. Option C confuses resource addressing (fixed versus parameterized URI) with payload shape; a direct resource can happily return a serialized list. Option D drags the model into an app-controlled rendering path where it has no role.

column2:
A teammate's pull request adds a templated resource docs://documents/{doc_id}/archive whose handler moves the document into an archive store and returns a confirmation string, so that 'the app can archive things with a single resource read.'

What is the main design problem?

A. The URI has too many path segments, because a resource template may carry only one placeholder and that placeholder must be the final segment.
B. Archiving must be exposed as a prompt instead, because a person ultimately initiates the action and prompts are the user-controlled primitive.
C. Resources exist to expose data for reading, so an operation with side effects like archiving belongs in a tool as an explicit action.
D. The handler returns a plain string, but resource handlers are required to return JSON so that clients can deserialize them by declared MIME type.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. Resources are the read primitive — clients ask for data at a URI and expect the fetch to be safe — so hiding a mutation behind a read breaks the contract every client assumes; state-changing operations are what tools are for. Option A invents template restrictions; placeholders may appear in any segment and a template is not limited to one. Option B confuses surfacing with execution — a user-initiated flow may be started via a prompt, but the archive operation itself would still run as a tool, not as the prompt. Option D is false; MIME types exist precisely because resources legitimately return plain text, JSON, or other formats.

Your ticket application needs two behaviors: rendering the current ticket queue in a sidebar whenever the app refreshes it, and letting Claude change a ticket's status mid-conversation once a customer's issue is resolved.

Which TWO primitive choices are correct? (Select TWO.)

A. Expose the queue as a resource that application code reads directly each time it refreshes the sidebar.
B. Expose the queue as a tool so the model can fetch it whenever it believes the sidebar has gone stale.
C. Expose status changes as a prompt that returns the updated ticket inside a pre-written assistant message.
D. Expose status changes as a tool that the model invokes with a ticket ID and the new status value.
column3:
Correct Answer: A and D. Option A matches the queue to the app-controlled primitive: the application knows when it refreshes the sidebar and simply reads the data, with no model involved. Option D matches the status change to the model-controlled primitive: deciding mid-conversation that a ticket is resolved is exactly the judgment tools delegate to Claude. Option B hands UI freshness to the model, which is not even running when the app repaints and has no visibility into the sidebar. Option C misuses prompts, which are user-invoked message templates — they deliver instructions to the model and cannot themselves execute a state change.

Support leads want a 'draft escalation email' action in your chat client: an operator explicitly triggers it from a menu, and Claude then walks through gathering the case details and writing the email in the team's standard format.

Which MCP primitive fits this feature?

A. A tool that Claude calls to start the escalation workflow whenever it detects rising frustration in the conversation.
B. A prompt that the client surfaces as a command or button and that returns the messages driving the escalation workflow.
C. A resource containing the email template that the application fetches at session start and displays for the operator to fill in.
D. A dedicated escalation agent that watches each conversation and takes over whenever escalation seems warranted.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. The defining requirement is that a person initiates the workflow, and user-controlled invocation is precisely what prompts are for: the client exposes them as buttons or slash commands, and invoking one returns curated messages that drive the multi-step task. Option A moves the trigger to the model and uses inferred sentiment as the signal, when the requirement is an explicit operator action. Option C supplies static data but no invocable workflow. Option D is heavy over-engineering — a monitoring agent — for what a predefined, user-triggered prompt already does.

column2:
Your team maintains the MCP server behind a document chatbot. Users can already type 'convert report.pdf to Markdown' and usually get an acceptable result. A teammate therefore argues that adding a server prompt, /format, for conversions would add nothing.

What is the strongest counterargument?

A. The prompt lets Claude decide by itself when a conversion is needed, which a typed request does not allow.
B. The prompt runs the conversion on the server itself, so the workflow finishes without a model turn or model tokens.
C. The prompt is written, tested and evaluated by the server team, so results depend less on each user's wording.
D. The prompt gives the client a way to pass arguments such as a document name, which a typed request has no place for.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. The point of MCP prompts is to package the server author's prompt-engineering expertise: a tuned, evaluated instruction outperforms the average user's ad hoc phrasing, and shipping it with the server raises the floor for everyone. Option A confuses the primitives: prompts are user-controlled, selected explicitly by a person, and it is tools that the model decides to call. Option B misunderstands the mechanism; a prompt returns messages and Claude still performs the work, tools included. Option D invents a gap: the typed request in the scenario already names the document, so nothing is missing for a prompt argument to supply.

column2:
Your /format slash command, which invokes an MCP prompt on your docs server, works, but every invocation reformats report.pdf regardless of which document the user selects, because the document name is written directly into the prompt template string on the server.

What is the correct mechanism for making the prompt document-specific?

A. Have the client string-replace report.pdf with the selected document name in the returned messages before sending them to Claude.
B. Define one prompt per document, such as format_report and format_plan, each with its own template and its own command.
C. Send the prompt as is and let Claude ask the user which document they meant in a follow-up turn before it tries to read anything.
D. Declare a doc_id argument on the prompt and have the client send the document the user selected in its prompts/get request.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. Prompts are parameterized templates: the client sends argument values with the get-prompt request, the server interpolates them into the template, and the returned messages arrive ready to send — that round trip is the designed mechanism for dynamic content. Option A makes every client reverse-engineer the template's internals, breaking the encapsulation that lets any client use the server's prompts. Option B multiplies prompts per document and goes stale the moment documents are added. Option C spends an extra model turn recovering information the user already provided at invocation time.

column2:
You shipped generate_weekly_report as a tool on your analytics MCP server. Logs show Claude occasionally invoking it mid-conversation when users merely mention the word 'report,' and stakeholders want the workflow to run only when a person explicitly asks for it.

What is the best architectural change?

A. Re-expose the workflow as an MCP prompt surfaced as a slash command, so that it starts only when a user deliberately invokes it.
B. Keep the tool and add a system-prompt rule stating that it must only be called when the user has explicitly requested a weekly report.
C. Keep the tool but require the model to state its confidence that a report is wanted, invoking it only when that confidence is above 90%.
D. Move the workflow into a resource that the application fetches automatically every Monday morning and injects into the conversation.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. The problem is invocation authority: a tool is model-controlled by definition, so as long as the workflow is a tool the model may fire it on a hunch; re-modeling it as a prompt makes invocation user-controlled, which is exactly the stakeholder requirement. Option B leaves the authority with the model and papers over it with prompt instructions that will probabilistically fail. Option C gates the decision on self-reported confidence, an unreliable signal that still leaves the model in charge. Option D changes the trigger to a schedule nobody asked for, and resources expose data rather than multi-step workflows.

column2:
While testing /format, an MCP prompt on your docs server, a developer inspects the get-prompt response expecting to find the reformatted document. Instead it contains a single user message instructing Claude to fetch the document with the server's read tool, rewrite it in Markdown, and save it with the server's edit tool. They file a bug titled 'prompt did not do anything.'

What should you explain?

A. The server is misconfigured; a correctly configured server executes the prompt's instructions itself and returns the finished document instead.
B. The prompt is missing a MIME type declaration, so the client cannot decode the finished Markdown document that the response actually carries.
C. This is correct behavior: a prompt returns messages for the client to send to Claude, and the work then happens through tool calls.
D. The prompt should be converted into a templated resource, since only resources are able to return document contents to the client.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. Prompts are pre-written conversation inputs, not remote procedures: get-prompt hands back messages, the client forwards them to Claude, and Claude then does the actual reading, rewriting, and saving via tools. Option A inverts the contract — get-prompt only renders the messages, and no server carries out the instructions they contain. Option B borrows MIME types from resources; a text message in a prompt needs no MIME type, and the response carries instructions rather than a finished document. Option D swaps in the read primitive when the feature is a workflow: a resource could serve the raw document but could never orchestrate reformatting and saving it.

column2:
Your client renders its slash-command autocomplete from a hardcoded array containing only 'format'. The server team ships new summarize and translate prompts; users of your client never see them, while another team's client offers all three immediately.

What change brings your client in line with intended MCP behavior?

A. Subscribe to the server team's release notes and update the hardcoded command array each sprint, shipping a client release for each new prompt.
B. Call the list-prompts operation when the session connects and build the command menu from the result, re-listing on each new session.
C. Ask the model at session start to guess which prompts the server most likely provides, and render its answer as the command menu.
D. Read the server's source files from disk at startup and parse the decorator names into a command list, so the menu tracks the code.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. Prompts are discoverable the same way tools are: the client asks the server what it offers via list-prompts and renders its UI from the live answer, which is why the other client picked up all three commands with zero changes. Option A institutionalizes manual synchronization and guarantees lag. Option C invites hallucinated commands; the model has no knowledge of a server's prompt catalog. Option D breaks the protocol boundary entirely and is impossible for any server that is not running from local source.

You are adding three tools to a new docs MCP server built with the Python SDK. Your only test path today is launching the full CLI chatbot, chatting until Claude happens to call each tool, and reading logs — roughly ten minutes per iteration, with API costs on every run.

What is the standard faster loop?

A. After each edit, run scripted evals that send the schemas in the tools parameter with sample prompts and grade whether the right tool was called.
B. Add logging calls to every tool and keep exercising them through chatbot conversations, reading the log output once the chatbot finishes each run.
C. Register the server with claude mcp add and ask Claude Code to call each tool from an interactive session, checking results by eye.
D. Launch the MCP Inspector with mcp dev on the server file and use it in the browser to list the tools and invoke each with chosen parameters.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. The Inspector exists for exactly this: an in-browser debugger, launched with the Python SDK's mcp dev command or directly with npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector, that connects to your server so you can invoke tools directly with hand-picked inputs and see results immediately, before any client integration. Option A keeps the model in the loop for what is currently a server-correctness question, slower and costlier than direct invocation. Option B adds visibility, and logging is the right way to log from a stdio server because it writes to stderr, but it leaves the ten-minute, conversation-driven cycle intact. Option C swaps one chat client for another: Claude must still decide to call each tool, so every iteration keeps the model's latency and API cost.

Which risk can the Inspector directly validate?

A. That each tool executes correctly when invoked with valid parameters and returns the expected output.
B. That Claude will select search_tickets rather than get_ticket_details when users ask keyword questions.
C. That the server sustains 50 concurrent client connections without latency regressions under load.
D. That the production client's session cleanup logic closes its connections properly on shutdown.

Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. The Inspector connects you directly to the server and lets you manually invoke its tools, resources, and prompts with chosen inputs and observe the results — so per-tool execution correctness is squarely within its scope. Option B is a model-behavior question; the Inspector never involves Claude, so tool selection can only be tested with the model in the loop. Option C is a load-testing concern beyond a manual, single-user debugger. Option D lives in the client codebase, which the Inspector replaces rather than exercises.

column2:
In the MCP Inspector you connect to your docs server and list its resources. The listing shows only docs://documents; your new templated resource docs://documents/{doc_id} is absent, and you begin suspecting the decorator is broken.

What is the most likely explanation?

A. Templated resources appear in the listing once a real client has called resources/read on one of their URIs at least once.
B. Direct resources and resource templates are listed by separate requests, and the template appears under the templates listing instead.
C. The Inspector cannot exercise templated resources, whose parameters are supplied by a model at run time rather than by a person.
D. A resource has to declare an application/json MIME type before the Inspector displays it in a listing, and this template declares none.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. Fixed-URI resources and resource templates are enumerated by separate requests. resources/list returns only the fixed-URI ones, while templates come back from resources/templates/list, so a template missing from the plain resource listing is expected, and the Inspector's Resources tab shows both kinds. Option A invents a usage precondition that does not exist. Option C is backwards; nothing about a template requires a model, and any client can fill in doc_id and read the resulting URI. Option D confuses the MIME type, a hint about how to interpret the payload, with visibility in listings.

column2:
Your docs MCP server's edit_document tool returns only a success message, never the document text; a separate read_doc_contents tool returns a document's text. You are investigating a report that some edits do not stick, and you want to confirm in the MCP Inspector whether a specific find-and-replace actually changed the stored document.

What is the right verification flow?

A. Run edit_document in the Inspector's Tools tab with the target parameters and treat its success message as proof that the document changed.
B. Run the same edit through the production chatbot and ask Claude to confirm in its reply whether the edit worked as intended on that document.
C. In the Inspector, run edit_document with the target parameters, then call read_doc_contents on the same document and check for the change.
D. Run edit_document in the Inspector with the target parameters, then search the Logs tab for the changed text in the messages the server emits.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. Because the edit tool's return value only signals that it ran, verifying the side effect means reading the state back: invoke the edit, then the read tool on the same document, and compare — a two-step check the Inspector supports because you invoke both tools by hand. Option A trusts a success message to prove a content change that the message does not contain. Option B substitutes the model's self-report for direct observation. Option D looks for evidence in the Logs tab, which shows only the notifications/message output that the server chooses to emit; nothing guarantees that it holds the stored text, so it cannot confirm that the edit stuck.

column2:
Your hand-rolled MCP client spawns a server subprocess and immediately writes a bare list-tools request to its stdin, with no other messages and no request metadata. The request hangs or comes back as an error, while a reference client built on the official SDK works against the same server every time.

Which step is your client missing?

A. Adding a fixed two-second delay between launching the subprocess and writing the first list-tools request to the pipe that feeds its stdin.
B. Retrying the list-tools request with exponential backoff until the server starts answering, and giving up after several attempts.
C. Switching the server from stdio to Streamable HTTP and delivering the same list-tools request as an HTTP POST to a single endpoint.
D. Telling the server which protocol version and capabilities the client supports, in the form that server's protocol revision requires.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. An MCP server has to know which protocol version the client speaks and what capabilities it has before it will serve operational requests such as list-tools. In protocol revisions up to 2025-11-25 the client supplies this once, in an initialize request that the server answers with its own capabilities, followed by an initialized notification. In the 2026-07-28 revision that handshake is gone, and every request carries the version and client capabilities in its _meta field instead. A bare request does neither, whereas the SDK client works out which form the server expects when it connects. Options A and B treat a protocol precondition as a timing flake; delays and retries cannot supply information the request never carries. Option C changes the transport even though the reference client works against the same server, so the transport is not what is missing: an HTTP POST would carry the same bare request with none of the version or capability information.

column2:
Your client assumes every MCP server implements tools, resources, and prompts. Connected to a minimal tools-only server, it calls list-prompts at startup and treats the resulting failure as fatal — aborting the session even though every tool works.

What is the correct fix?

A. Read the server's declared capabilities and exercise only the features that it actually advertises.
B. Require server teams to implement all three primitives before your client will accept a connection to them.
C. Wrap list-prompts in a retry loop, since prompt support may finish loading shortly after server startup.
D. Delegate the check to the model by asking Claude at session start whether this server provides prompts.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. Tools, resources and prompts are optional features, each server declares which of them it supports, and a well-behaved client consults that declaration instead of assuming the full set. The declaration arrives in the initialize response under handshake-based protocol revisions and in the server/discover result under the 2026-07-28 revision, and the SDK exposes it on the client once it has connected. Option B inverts the fix by demanding servers change to satisfy a faulty client assumption; the primitives are optional by design. Option C misreads a permanent capability absence as a transient warm-up condition. Option D asks the model to know something it cannot observe; capability information arrives through the protocol, not the conversation.

column2:
Your CLI chatbot connects to your docs MCP server successfully, but Claude answers every document question from general knowledge and never calls the server's read tool. Request logs show each call to Claude contains only the system prompt and the user's message.

What is the first thing to fix in the loop?

A. Add a line to the system prompt telling Claude that a document server is connected and that it should call the read tool for document questions.
B. Fetch the server's tool definitions through the client's list-tools function and pass them in the tools parameter of each request to Claude.
C. Set tool_choice to any on each request to Claude, forcing a tool call whenever a document question comes in instead of an answer from memory.
D. Have the server send notifications/tools/list_changed straight to Claude whenever the documents change, bypassing the client loop.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. A model can only use tools that are passed to it in the request; the loop must first gather the server's tools via the client and send them alongside the query, which is precisely the step this codebase skipped. Option A tells the model tools exist without giving it any to call — there is still nothing in the request to select. Option C forces a tool call, but tool_choice: any only makes Claude use one of the tools provided in the request, and this request provides none. Option D misreads a real notification: notifications/tools/list_changed signals a change in the server's tool list to the client, and servers never talk to the model, so the client still has to put the tool definitions into each request.

column2:
In your agent loop, Claude responds with a tool-use request for read_doc_contents, and your client executes it through call-tool and receives the document text. But the chat then stalls: the transcript ends at Claude's tool-use turn, and in 100% of tool-using conversations the user sees no answer.

What is missing from the loop?

A. A larger max_tokens setting that lets the final answer fit into the same response as the tool call instead of being cut off.
B. A parser that pulls Claude's final answer text out of the tool_use block itself, where it is embedded alongside the call.
C. Sending the tool's output back to Claude as a tool result and continuing the loop while the stop reason is tool_use.
D. A line in the system prompt telling Claude to answer the question and call the tool within a single turn of the conversation.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. A tool-use response is the midpoint of the cycle, not the end: the client must execute the call, return the result to the model in the next message, and keep looping while the stop reason is tool_use, so the model can give its final answer once it stops requesting tools — this loop executes the tool but never completes the round trip. Option A misdiagnoses; no answer was truncated because none has been generated yet. Option B tries to parse an answer out of a message that by definition contains a request, not a conclusion. Option D asks the model to answer before it has the document, which is the situation tools exist to prevent.

column2:
A nightly batch job opens a fresh connection to your stdio MCP server for each of 500 documents, calling the Python SDK's connection functions by hand and never closing what it opens. Over the run it leaves more and more orphaned server subprocesses behind, and the job increasingly hangs at exit.

Which practice addresses this?

A. Scope each connection in an async context manager whose exit owns the cleanup, so each transport and subprocess is released when its document is done.
B. Let the operating system reap the orphaned subprocesses when the job's main process finally exits, since stdio servers hold no other resources.
C. Leave the connections open, since the SDK closes each transport and its subprocess automatically once the client object is garbage collected.
D. Add a scheduled task on the machine that kills any stray server processes once every hour, so the job never accumulates more than an hour's worth.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. A stdio connection holds a live subprocess and its pipes, which need deterministic teardown, and the standard practice is to scope each connection in an async context manager so that leaving the block closes the transport and shuts the subprocess down even when an error interrupts the work. Option B waits on an exit that the leaked resources are themselves preventing. Option C bets on garbage collection to perform cleanup that the SDK ties to leaving the context manager. Option D is out-of-band process killing that treats the symptom while the job keeps leaking. Currency note (Oct 2026): Python SDK 2.x provides this directly as async with Client(...), which owns the whole connection lifecycle, while ClientSession remains as the lower-level interface that older tutorials wrapped in a hand-written client class with connect and cleanup methods.

column2:
A code review of your team's custom agent, which uses tools from an internal MCP server, finds two problems: the tool schemas sent to Claude were copied into the codebase by hand months ago and no longer match the server, causing schema-mismatch failures in 9% of calls; and when Claude requests a tool, the agent runs its own local reimplementation of the tool's logic, which has drifted from the server's behavior.

Which TWO changes fix the architecture? (Select TWO.)

A. Paste the server's current schemas into the system prompt and diff them by hand against the server at each release, so drift is caught before deploy.
B. Cap the loop at one tool call per conversation to limit the blast radius of any remaining drift, and log every mismatch for manual review.
C. Fetch tool definitions from the server at session start through the client's list-tools call, so Claude always sees what the server currently exposes.
D. Route every tool-use request from Claude through the client's call-tool function, so the server executes its own tools and returns the results.
column3:
Correct Answer: C and D. Options C and D restore the two halves of MCP's contract: definitions are discovered live from the server rather than vendored, which ends schema drift, and execution happens on the server that owns the tools, which ends logic drift. Option A remains manual and stale, and the system prompt is not where tool definitions belong — they are structured request inputs, not prose. Option B is an iteration cap masquerading as safety; it truncates legitimate multi-step work while both kinds of drift continue on the one call it still allows.

column2:
Your team of eight shares one repository, and you want your internal docs MCP server offered in Claude Code to every engineer who clones the repository, without each of them having to add the server by hand. The server starts from a single launch command and needs no credentials.

How should the server be configured?

A. Each engineer adds the server at user scope, so that it follows them across all of their projects, including this repository.
B. Each engineer adds the server at local scope during onboarding, with the exact claude mcp add command documented in the README.
C. Add it at project scope, which writes it to a .mcp.json file at the repository root that is checked into version control.
D. Paste the server's launch command into the repository's CLAUDE.md, which is committed, so Claude Code starts the server when it is needed.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. Project scope exists for exactly this: the configuration lives in .mcp.json at the repository root, is committed like any other file, and every teammate who pulls the repo is offered the server, needing only to approve it when Claude Code prompts. Option A is per-person setup that also spreads a project-specific server into unrelated projects. Option B still requires all eight engineers to perform documented manual setup, which is what you are trying to eliminate. Option D puts a shell command into model instructions — CLAUDE.md guides Claude's behavior and does not register MCP servers with the client.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.4

References:
• Connect Claude Code to MCP — Project scope
• Connect Claude Code to MCP — Project server approvals and workspace trust

column2:
A security review flags your repository: the committed .mcp.json entry for your ticket-tracker MCP server contains a real API token in its env block. The team still wants the shared, checked-in configuration to keep working for everyone.

What is the correct remediation?

A. Reference the token as ${TRACKER_API_TOKEN} in .mcp.json, so the committed file expands a variable that each engineer sets locally.
B. Keep the token committed but restrict repository access to current team members, rotating the token whenever someone leaves.
C. Move the server entry to user scope on each laptop and share the token through the team chat during setup, keeping .mcp.json token-free.
D. Delete the env block and hardcode the token inside the server's own source code, which the security review did not scan.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. .mcp.json supports environment-variable expansion precisely so shared configuration can be committed without embedding secrets: the checked-in file references ${TRACKER_API_TOKEN}, and each engineer supplies their own value locally. Option B leaves a live credential in the repository and its history, which access controls do not cure. Option C abandons the shared config and distributes the secret over chat, trading one exposure for another. Option D relocates the hardcoded secret into committed source code — the same finding one directory over.

References:
• Connect Claude Code to MCP — Environment variable expansion in .mcp.json
• Connect Claude Code to MCP — Project scope

column2:
You built a personal scratchpad-notes MCP server and want it available in every Claude Code session on your laptop — client work, open source, everything — without touching any repository's shared configuration or re-adding it project by project.

Which configuration scope fits?

A. Project scope, adding the server to each repository's .mcp.json file whenever you first open that repository.
B. Local scope in each project, since the server itself runs locally on your laptop over the stdio transport.
C. Project scope inside a template repository from which all of your future projects are forked.
D. User scope, which registers the server once for you and makes it available in all of your projects.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. User scope is the cross-project, personal option: configured once, available in every project you open, and invisible to teammates' shared configuration. Option A repeats setup per repository and pushes your personal tooling into files the whole team shares. Option B conflates the scope named local with the transport — local scope is still per-project, so the server would need re-adding everywhere. Option C only covers repositories descended from the template and still edits shared project configuration to solve a personal need.

• Connect Claude Code to MCP — MCP installation scopes

column2:
A developer wires three MCP servers into Claude Code — internal docs, the ticket tracker, and a read-only database — then asks whether one conversation can pull a ticket, look up the customer in the database, and cite a runbook, or whether that takes three separate sessions.

What should you tell them?

A. One session per server: Claude Code binds each conversation to a single MCP connection at startup, chosen from the configured list.
B. One conversation works: the host holds a client connection to each server and offers the tools from all of them to the model together.
C. It can work in one session only if the three servers are first merged into a single server process that exposes all of the tools.
D. It works only if the user issues a command to switch the active server before each cross-server tool call, since one server is active at a time.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. The host creates one client per configured server and aggregates what they expose, so tools from all three servers are available to the model at the same time, whether loaded up front or found on demand through tool search, and can be chained freely within one conversation. Option A invents a one-connection-per-conversation restriction that contradicts the one-client-per-server architecture. Option C demands a server merge that the architecture makes unnecessary. Option D imagines a manual server-switching mode; selection happens per tool call by the model, not through user routing commands.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.4

References:
• MCP architecture — Participants
• MCP server concepts — Bringing servers together
• Connect Claude Code to MCP — Scale with MCP tool search

column2:
A docs MCP server that your team runs for a research agent exposes two tools. search_docs takes keywords and lists matching documents, identifying each by an eight-character short form of its ID. read_doc_contents returns one document by its full ID, and full IDs are between eight and twelve characters long. Each description runs to several sentences, and the second one states that the ID must be copied from a search_docs result. In test transcripts the agent searches first and passes the listed ID on unchanged, yet about 20% of reads fail with 'document not found'.

What is the most effective first change?

A. Rewrite both tool descriptions to state that read_doc_contents takes a full ID copied from a search result.
B. Add few-shot transcripts to the system prompt that show a search followed by a read with the listed ID.
C. Make read_doc_contents fall back to the closest-matching document when an ID does not resolve.
D. Change search_docs to include the document's full ID in each search result, ready to pass to a read.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. The descriptions are specific and the agent follows them: it searches first and passes on the ID exactly as listed. The failures come from the tools themselves. search_docs hands back an eight-character short form, read_doc_contents needs the full ID, and for a document whose ID is longer than eight characters the two do not match, which no wording can repair. Option D makes one tool's output a valid input for the other and removes the cause. Option A is the right first step when descriptions are minimal and the agent guesses IDs, but these descriptions already say this and are obeyed. Option B demonstrates a sequence that the agent performs in every transcript. Option C hides the defect and adds a worse one, because several documents can share a short form and the closest match may be the wrong document, returned without an error.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1

References:
• Define tools (schemas, descriptions) — Best practices for tool definitions
• MCP server concepts — How tools work

column2:
Your document MCP server has one search tool, search_docs. It takes a query string and an optional doc_type value (pdf, markdown or spreadsheet) and returns a list of document IDs and titles in the same shape for every type. Across 200 logged tasks, the model set doc_type correctly whenever a request implied a type and left it out otherwise. A teammate proposes replacing the tool with search_pdfs, search_markdown and search_spreadsheets, arguing that purpose-specific tools are easier for a model to choose between.

How should you respond to the proposal?

A. Keep the single search_docs tool with its optional doc_type parameter, and decline the split.
B. Replace search_docs with the three type-specific tools, each with its own detailed description.
C. Keep the single search_docs tool, and make doc_type a required parameter in its input schema.
D. Replace search_docs with the three tools, plus a system-prompt rule that maps each type to its tool.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. Splitting pays off when one generic tool hides several different operations with different inputs or outputs. search_docs performs one operation: every call takes a query and returns the same list, the document type is just a filter value, and the logs show that the model already handles it correctly. Three tools would do the same job with near-identical descriptions, and overlapping definitions are a known cause of misrouting; a search that implies no type would also need three calls. Option A keeps what works. Option B applies a rule meant for distinct operations where there is nothing distinct to separate. Option C keeps the tool but breaks the part that works: with doc_type required, a request that implies no type forces the model to pick one, which narrows a search the logs show it was right to leave open. Option D adds the overlap and then patches it with a keyword rule, the kind of system-prompt instruction that creates unintended tool associations, for example when a user mentions a PDF but wants every type searched.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1

References:
• Define tools (schemas, descriptions) — Best practices for tool definitions
• MCP server concepts — How tools work

column2:
A finance operations assistant answers staff questions about supplier invoices through two MCP tools: find_invoices, which searches by supplier name, and get_invoice, which returns one invoice by its number. Logs from 300 conversations show that the assistant chose the right tool and passed valid arguments every time. In 41 of those conversations it quoted an amount exactly 100 times too large. For an invoice of 1,250.00 euros, get_invoice returns {"total": 125000, "currency": "EUR"}. The whole of the tool's description is 'Returns an invoice by its number.'

What is the most likely root cause of the wrong amounts?

A. The descriptions of find_invoices and get_invoice overlap too much for the model to tell the tools apart.
B. The get_invoice description does not say what unit the total field of its result is expressed in.
C. The total field holds a six-digit figure, and the model's arithmetic on numbers of that size is unreliable.
D. The get_invoice input schema does not document the format that an invoice number has to take.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. The logs rule out problems with selection and inputs: the right tool was called with valid arguments in all 300 conversations. What the assistant lacks is a statement of what the result means. A total of 125000 beside the currency code EUR reads naturally as euros, and the one-line description does not say that the figure is in cents, so the assistant has to guess, and it guessed wrong 41 times (Option B). A description should say what a tool returns as well as when to call it; stating the unit, or returning a self-describing field, closes the gap. Options A and D describe failures that the logs show did not happen. Option C misreads the symptom: quoting an invoice total involves no arithmetic, and an error of exactly a factor of 100 points to a misread unit, not to unreliable handling of large numbers.

• MCP spec: tools — Tool

column2:
Your team's document assistant edits files through an edit_document MCP tool that performs exact find-and-replace with doc_id, old_string and new_string parameters. The old_string description states that the text must match the document exactly and be copied from a read of the document, and logs show that the model does this. About 6% of edits change nothing, all of them on documents that a colleague altered after the model had read them. The tool's result is the text 'Edit applied' in every case, and the assistant goes on to tell the user that the change has been made.

What is the most effective fix?

A. Expand the old_string description with an example of text copied verbatim, whitespace included, from a read.
B. Have the server fuzzy-match old_string and apply the replacement at the closest location it finds.
C. Return an isError: true result when old_string is not found, with text telling the model to re-read.
D. Have the server retry the edit up to five times with the same arguments when the document comes back unchanged.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. The model's arguments are right for the text it read; the document changed afterwards. The fault lies in what the tool reports: a replacement that matched nothing comes back as 'Edit applied', so the model has no way to know that it failed and passes a false success on to the user. Option C reports the failure as a tool execution error whose text names the cause and the next step, which lets the model read the document again and retry with current text. Option A restates a requirement that the description already makes and the model already meets. Option B guesses at a location in text that someone has just changed, replacing a detectable failure with a silent wrong edit. Option D resends arguments that will not match until the document is read again.
