References:
• MCP spec: tools — Error handling
• Text editor tool — Handle errors
• Handle tool calls — Handling errors with is_error

column2:
Two failure modes account for the errors from get_ticket, a tracker MCP tool that your support agent uses to read tickets. Upstream timeouts make up about 60% of them and usually clear within seconds. The other 40% are requests for tickets in a restricted legal project that the agent's service account is not allowed to read; in those cases the ticket ID is valid and the ticket exists. Both failures return 'Error: request failed.' The agent abandons timed-out requests that a retry would have completed, and after a failure on a restricted ticket it retries several times and then starts trying other ticket IDs.

How should the server's error results change?

A. Mark timeouts as transient and retryable, and restricted tickets as validation errors that request a corrected ticket ID.
B. Mark timeouts as transient and retryable, and restricted tickets as permission errors that are not retryable, with a reason.
C. Mark both failures as transient and retryable, and have the client retry each one three times before the model sees it.
D. Mark timeouts as transient and retryable, and return restricted tickets as a successful result with an empty ticket.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. The two failures call for opposite responses, and the second has nothing to do with the input: the ID is valid and the ticket exists, but the service account is not allowed to read it. That is a permission error. A retry will not change it and neither will another ID, so the result should say that it is not retryable and give a reason the agent can pass on or escalate, as Option B does, while timeouts stay transient and retryable. Option A's validation label tells the agent to find a corrected ID, which encourages the ID-guessing already seen. Option C spends retries on a failure that will not succeed and still tells the model nothing about it. Option D reports an access failure as an empty success, so the agent would treat an existing ticket as blank.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.2

References:
• MCP spec: tools — Error handling
• Handle tool calls — Handling errors with is_error

column2:
A travel-booking assistant finds fares through an MCP tool, search_fares, that queries three airline reservation systems and merges their answers. When one system times out, the tool's handler catches the exception, leaves that airline out, and returns the other two airlines' fares as an ordinary result. Few routes are served by all three airlines, so a result that lists two of them is common. During one six-hour period an airline's reservation system is unreachable, while its fares, often the lowest on its routes, remain on sale through other channels.

What will the assistant most likely do during those six hours?

A. Present the lowest fare in each result as the cheapest one available on that route.
B. Tell travellers that one airline's fares were not checked for their route.
C. Retry each search several times and then report that fare search is unavailable.
D. Stop answering fare questions until the unreachable system is back in service.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. The assistant can act only on what the tool result tells it, and this result says that nothing is wrong: the handler catches the timeout and returns two airlines' fares in the ordinary form, on routes where two airlines is a normal answer. The assistant therefore treats each list as complete and presents its lowest fare as the cheapest (Option A). Option B assumes a signal that the result does not carry. Option C describes what would follow if the tool reported the failure, but the handler suppresses it and the model sees no error. Option D is wrong for the same reason: the exception is caught inside the handler, so nothing interrupts the conversation. The remedy is to return the fares that were found together with a note naming the system that failed, that the failure is a timeout, and that a retry may succeed.

column2:
Your team's repository has a committed .mcp.json that defines a ticket-tracker MCP server, run as a local process, and the entry's env block sets the server's API token to ${TRACKER_API_TOKEN}. Seven engineers use the server in Claude Code every day. An engineer who joined this week clones the repository and approves the server when Claude Code asks, but the tracker rejects every tool call as unauthenticated, and claude mcp list shows a missing-variable warning for the server. Team policy is that credentials are never committed.

What is the correct fix?

A. Add a :- default holding a working token to the committed ${TRACKER_API_TOKEN} reference.
B. Run claude mcp reset-project-choices on the new laptop and approve the tracker server again.
C. Move the server out of .mcp.json and have each engineer add it at user scope with a token.
D. Set TRACKER_API_TOKEN to the new engineer's own token in the shell that launches Claude Code.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. Expansion keeps the secret out of the repository by leaving it out of the file: the committed entry only names a variable, and Claude Code fills in the value from each engineer's own environment when it loads the configuration. The new laptop has no such variable, which is what the warning reports, so the server is started with the unexpanded text in place of a token and the tracker rejects it. Option D supplies the variable on that machine and leaves the shared file alone. Option A would make the reference resolve, but by committing a live credential, which the policy forbids and expansion exists to prevent. Option B resets approval choices, and approval is not the problem: the server was approved and is running. Option C discards a shared definition that works for seven engineers in order to repair one machine.

column2:
A docs chatbot that your team runs answers questions over about 12,000 internal documents served by an MCP server. When a user names a document with an @ mention, the application reads it as an MCP resource and places its contents in the prompt. Transcript analysis shows that in 70% of conversations the user names no document and asks open questions, many of which depend on what was said before, such as 'and does that apply to contractors?' In those conversations the chatbot's model calls a search_docs tool with keywords of its own choosing and then reads the best match. A teammate proposes removing the tool and handling these conversations with resource reads as well, to save the two tool round trips.

What is the best response to the proposal?

A. Adopt it, and replace search_docs with a resource read of the best-matching document.
B. Adopt it, and replace search_docs with a resource that lists the 12,000 titles in each prompt.
C. Reject it, and keep search_docs as a tool that the model calls with a query it writes itself.
D. Reject it, and turn search_docs into an MCP prompt that users select before they ask a question.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. Resources suit data that the application is able to select without the model: after an @ mention it knows exactly which document to fetch. In these conversations nothing names a document, and many questions make sense only in light of what was said before, so there is nothing deterministic to read. Turning the conversation into a search query, and judging which hit answers it, is contextual work for the model, and model-controlled operations are what tools are for (Option C). Option A assumes the application already knows the best-matching document, which is the very thing the search establishes. Option B puts 12,000 titles into every request and still leaves the chosen document to be read. Option D makes users trigger a search by hand, when they ask in plain language and expect the chatbot to look things up.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.4

References:
• MCP server concepts — Core server features
• MCP spec: tools — User interaction model
• MCP spec: resources — User interaction model

column2:
An analytics assistant that your data team built writes SQL against a reporting database through an MCP server. The database has 28 tables, and its schema changes a few times a year. Traces show that nearly every task opens the same way: one list_tables call and then four or five describe_table calls before the assistant writes its first query. Those opening calls make up about 40% of all tool calls and most of the delay that users notice. The server exposes tools and nothing else, and the full schema is a small fraction of the assistant's context window.

Which MCP design fits this need best?

A. A resource holding the schema catalog, which the application reads at session start and places in context.
B. A prompt named explore_schema, which users select at session start to have the tables described.
C. A single run_sql tool with the schema tools removed, which leaves table names to be learned from errors.
D. A dedicated description tool for each of the 28 tables, which replaces the one tool that takes a table name.
column3:
Correct Answer: A. The schema is a small, stable catalog that almost every task needs, and the assistant keeps rediscovering it through the same exploratory calls. Exposing it as an MCP resource lets the application load it once per session, so the assistant sees which tables and columns exist before it writes anything (Option A); resources are the primitive for read-only context such as database schemas. Option B still runs the exploration and makes it depend on a person remembering to select a prompt. Option C removes the calls by removing the information, which trades them for failed queries. Option D multiplies the tool list by 28 and leaves the assistant making the same lookups, one call per table.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.4

References:
• MCP server concepts — Core server features
• MCP spec: resources — User interaction model
• Connect Claude Code to MCP — Use MCP resources

column2:
Stakeholders want Claude to produce your analytics team's weekly report whenever a user asks for it in conversation, with no command to learn. The workflow ships on your analytics MCP server as a prompt, which your chat client surfaces as the slash command /weekly_report. The report is read-only and takes a few seconds to produce. Logs show that in about a third of sessions users ask for it in plain language, as in 'can you pull together this week's numbers?', and Claude replies that it has no way to generate the report.

What is the best architectural change?

A. Keep the prompt, and rename the command to something shorter that users find easier to type.
B. Move the workflow into a resource that the application reads at the start of each session.
C. Keep the prompt, and add a system-prompt rule telling Claude to run /weekly_report on request.
D. Expose the workflow as a generate_weekly_report tool whose description states when to use it.
column3:
Correct Answer: D. The requirement is about who starts the workflow. A prompt is user-controlled: it runs when a person selects it, so a request made in ordinary conversation does not trigger it. A tool is model-controlled, which means Claude is able to decide from the conversation that the report is wanted and call it, as Option D provides; because the report is read-only and quick, an occasional unneeded run costs little. Option A keeps the dependence on a command that users are not typing. Option B loads something at every session start instead of running the workflow on request, and a resource supplies data, not a workflow carried out on demand. Option C asks Claude to trigger something that this client runs when a user selects it; an instruction does not give the model that ability.

References:
• MCP server concepts — Core server features
• MCP spec: tools — User interaction model
• MCP spec: prompts — User interaction model

column2:
In a design review for a GitHub-connected release assistant, your team lists what the assistant has to do. Reading pull requests, posting review comments and checking CI status are standard repository operations, and the GitHub MCP server that the team already uses provides them. The assistant must also run the team's own release-gate check, which compares a release candidate with an in-house change-approval database and a deploy-freeze calendar that exist only inside your company. One engineer proposes writing a single custom MCP server that implements everything, GitHub operations included, to have it all in one place.

Which approach should the team take?

A. Write the single custom server, with the GitHub operations and the release-gate check side by side.
B. Use the existing GitHub server alone, and have Claude infer approval from pull-request labels.
C. Keep the existing GitHub server, and build a small custom server for the release-gate check alone.
D. Skip MCP for the release gate, and describe the approval and freeze rules in the system prompt.
column3:
Correct Answer: C. The two needs fall on opposite sides of one rule: use an existing server for a standard integration, and write a custom one for work that is specific to your team. The repository operations are standard and a maintained server already provides them, while the release gate depends on an approval database and a freeze calendar that exist only inside the company, which an outside server has no way to reach. Option C reuses the first and builds only the second. Option A has the team rewrite GitHub tooling and then maintain it through every change to the GitHub API. Option B leaves Claude inferring approval from indirect signs, when the check exists to gate releases on recorded approvals and freeze dates. Option D supplies rules but no access to the live approval records or the calendar that the check has to read.

Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.4

References:
• MCP example servers — Official integrations
• Connect Claude Code to MCP — Find and build MCP servers
• Connect Claude Code to MCP — Example: Connect to GitHub for code reviews

column2:
You are evaluating a database MCP server in Claude Code for one client's repository. Its launch command includes a connection string with your personal read-only credentials for that client's staging database. You want the server in your own sessions in that repository and nowhere else: it should stay out of your other clients' projects, and teammates who work on the repository should neither see it nor be asked to approve it. The repository already has a committed .mcp.json that the whole team shares.

Which configuration scope fits?

A. User scope, with the server stored in your ~/.claude.json for use across your projects.
B. Local scope, with the server stored in your ~/.claude.json under this project's path.
C. Project scope, with the server added to the repository's committed .mcp.json file.
D. Project scope, with the server added to .mcp.json on a personal branch kept unmerged.
column3:
Correct Answer: B. Two requirements decide this: the server has to stay private to you, and it has to load in one repository and nowhere else. Local scope, the default for claude mcp add, meets both: the entry is stored in your ~/.claude.json under that project's path, stays out of version control, and does not appear in your other projects (Option B). Option A is private, but user scope loads the server in every project you open, other clients' repositories included. Option C shares the server with the whole team and commits a connection string that holds your credentials. Option D still commits those credentials, and the server disappears whenever you switch branches. Currency note (Oct 2026): the exam guide contrasts project-level .mcp.json with user-level ~/.claude.json; current docs divide the personal side into local scope (one project) and user scope (all projects), both stored in ~/.claude.json.
